operationalization: Across well-studied structures, partition phenotypic variation into direct environmental plasticity and evolved, heritable effects, and test whether climate or food alone predicts complex functional matching. Persistence of matching after common-environment and phylogenetic controls would refute the proposed external-only explanation.
obstacles: The universal scope cannot be exhaustively sampled.
Historical causes are confounded with present-day function.
rationale: Morphology, interactions and some common-garden data are public, but no integrated dataset spans complex adaptations generally. Restricted comparative tests are feasible, while excluding every external-condition account is difficult.

operationalization: Estimate lifetime reproductive success or survival as a function of a measured heritable trait under density limitation. A consistently positive selection differential for profitable variants, coupled with excess offspring mortality, supports the claim; no differential refutes it in each tested population.

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database
candidate_datasets.role: population vital rates and demographic limitation

obstacles: Heritability and fitness are rarely measured together.
Results from monitored species cannot establish universality.
rationale: Standard demographic and selection analyses directly test the mechanism in many populations. Existing datasets have strong examples but cover only a small, nonrandom fraction of all organisms.

operationalization: Use time-calibrated phylogenies and fossils to test whether lineage divergence is associated with inferred selection and whether less-adapted lineages have elevated extinction. Patterns must exceed neutral diversification and environmental-turnover null models.
obstacles: Fitness of extinct forms is usually unobserved.
Diversification models have identifiability problems.
rationale: Divergence and extinction are measurable, but 'less improved' requires substantial reinterpretation. Fossil and phylogenetic data support restricted tests, not the claimed near-inevitability or attribution to selection.

operationalization: Compare independent molecular characters, shared derived genomic changes and fossil succession against separate-creation and common-descent models. Nested congruent ancestry across congeneric species supports descent; independent origins without shared history would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: temporal occurrence of ancestral and extinct forms

obstacles: Fossil ancestors are rarely identifiable with certainty.
Not every described species has genomic data.
rationale: Multiple large public resources contain independent molecular and fossil consequences of descent. Although complete species coverage is absent, the universal immutability alternative has clear, strongly discriminating tests.

operationalization: For many lineages, estimate the share of heritable phenotypic and genomic change attributable to positive or purifying selection versus drift, gene flow and other mechanisms. A majority attributable to selection would support 'main,' whereas consistently minority contributions would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: population genomic data for selection inference

obstacles: 'Main' lacks a unique denominator.
Selection and demography can produce similar genomic signals.
Available taxa are highly biased.
rationale: Mechanism-specific evidence exists, but aggregating all species modification into comparable causal shares is not currently possible. Existing data resolve selected lineages and traits only.

operationalization: Compare within-population phenotypic or genomic variance in matched domesticated and wild taxa using common trait scales and hierarchical models. Greater variance across most matched pairs supports the generalization; equal or lower domestic variance refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Genesys PGR
candidate_datasets.role: crop accession phenotypes and passport data

obstacles: Management populations and wild populations are not sampled comparably.
Trait choice strongly affects variance.
rationale: The comparison is direct and standard, and substantial public domestic data exist. Matched individual-level wild data across plants and animals are incomplete, limiting the stated breadth.

operationalization: Across matched domestic lineages, regress heritable variation on quantified environmental heterogeneity and difference from ancestral habitat while controlling population size, admixture and selection. A positive independent effect supports the mechanism; its absence or dominance by breeding history refutes it.
obstacles: Artificial selection and admixture confound environmental effects.
Ancestral husbandry environments are poorly documented.
rationale: Variables can be approximated, but historical exposure and causal attribution are weakly recorded. Existing crop and climate data permit only restricted, confounded tests.

operationalization: Compare de novo mutation, epimutation and offspring variance after documented preconception environmental exposures of both parents, against unexposed controls and effects arising after conception. Predominantly preconception-mediated variance would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: public gamete and parental-exposure molecular studies

obstacles: Exposure, gamete state and offspring phenotype are rarely linked.
The proposed predominance requires representative cross-taxon data.
rationale: Modern parental-exposure studies can test specific cases, but public data are fragmented and molecular proxies do not establish the most frequent cause of organismal variability. A representative coordinated dataset would be needed.

operationalization: Test whether parental use or disuse predicts offspring skeletal traits after controlling offspring activity, genotype and maternal environment, ideally across pedigrees or reciprocal interventions. Inheritance of the acquired shift supports the claim; disappearance under controls refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public experimental and pedigree phenotype datasets

obstacles: Domestic-wild differences reflect genetic selection and development.
Few public multigenerational intervention datasets exist.
rationale: The inherited acquired-effect mechanism has a clear experimental test, and some relevant data are public. Existing comparative skeleton data alone cannot identify use and disuse as the cause.

operationalization: Estimate genetic correlations and correlated responses between deliberately selected traits and unselected traits in breeding populations. Nonzero repeatable correlated responses support the claim; consistently independent traits would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: mapped pleiotropic and correlated production traits

obstacles: Linkage can mimic pleiotropic correlation.
The phrase 'almost certainly' requires broad sampling.
rationale: Multi-trait pedigrees, genomic associations and selection experiments directly measure correlated response. Public livestock and crop data provide enough breadth for a strong present-day test, though not every selection regime.

operationalization: In pedigrees with longitudinal phenotyping, compare age of onset of a heritable trait in parents and offspring against shuffled parent-offspring pairs. Positive age concordance supports the rule; no concordance refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: longitudinal pedigree datasets from individual studies

obstacles: Age of first parental appearance is rarely recorded.
Disease onset is an imperfect proxy for any peculiarity.
rationale: The statistic is straightforward, but datasets linking pedigrees to repeated age-specific traits are scattered and biased toward disease. Only limited domains can be tested now.

operationalization: Embed standardized morphology and fertility of domestic races and closely allied wild species in the same multivariate trait space. Compare effect sizes and directions of divergence; similar axes but usually smaller race distances support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genetic distances among breeds and congeners

obstacles: 'Same manner' permits multiple metrics.
Cross-fertility data are sparse and nonstandard.
rationale: Public morphology and sequence data support broad comparisons, but fertility, monstrosity and uniformity are not integrated. Conclusions will depend on trait and distance definitions.

operationalization: Randomly sample many wild species across clades, maintain them under comparable domestication for the same number of generations, and compare standardized heritable variance with established domestic progenitors. Comparable mean variance would support the prediction.
obstacles: The required counterfactual domestication histories do not exist.
Survivorship and domestication feasibility would bias species selection.
rationale: The prediction is measurable but explicitly requires long, matched domestication experiments on a representative set of wild species. Existing domestication episodes are selected, heterogeneous and too few for the proposed counterfactual.

operationalization: Fit demographic ancestry models to whole genomes from global dogs and candidate wild canids, testing one-source against multiple-species ancestry. Significant ancestry from several distinct wild species supports the claim; a single ancestral species with later limited introgression refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: public dog and wild-canid whole-genome reads

candidate_datasets.name: European Nucleotide Archive
candidate_datasets.role: independent archive of canid genomic datasets

obstacles: Ancient introgression can be confused with multiple domestication sources.
Extinct source populations may be unsampled.
rationale: Extensive modern and ancient canid genomes are public, and standard admixture and demographic models directly distinguish the alternatives. Residual ambiguity concerns semantics of descent and extinct sources, not data availability.

operationalization: Compare whole genomes of diverse domestic pigeon breeds with Columba livia subspecies and other candidate wild stocks using phylogenetic and admixture models. Nesting of all breeds within rock-pigeon diversity supports the claim; a distinct ancestral contribution would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: public domestic and wild pigeon genomes

obstacles: Some geographic wild populations remain undersampled.
Recent introgression must be distinguished from primary ancestry.
rationale: The historical alternatives have direct genomic predictions and broad public sampling. Standard phylogenomics and ancestry inference can resolve the claim with high power.

operationalization: For breeds with archived genomes and histories, test for sequential allele-frequency shifts and polygenic selection in directions matching documented human preferences, versus sudden-origin or neutral models. Repeated cumulative directional change supports accumulative selection.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal QTLdb
candidate_datasets.role: domestic trait loci and selection targets

obstacles: Historical breeding records are incomplete.
Selection, drift and introgression can generate overlapping signatures.
rationale: Genomic time series and breeding records test several emblematic breeds, but historical coverage is uneven. The broad claim that this was the key cause across domestic forms is only partially resolvable.

operationalization: For crop varieties grouped by documented selection target, compare among-race standardized divergence in selected organs with divergence in unselected organs. Predominantly greater divergence in the selected part supports the rule; comparable divergence elsewhere refutes it.
obstacles: Phenotyping protocols differ among collections.
Correlated traits may blur organ-specific effects.
rationale: Large germplasm repositories contain multi-organ traits across many cultivated varieties, and the required variance comparison is standard. Historical target labels are imperfect but enough major crops are documented for a decisive general test.

operationalization: Use historical pedigrees, phenotypes and genomes to test whether preferential reproduction of higher-performing individuals predicts directional breed change despite no formal breeding goal. Sustained response matching selection differentials supports the mechanism.
obstacles: Intentions of historical breeders are unobserved.
Long time series with both parent choice and phenotype are rare.
rationale: Selection response is testable, but classifying it as unconscious and extending it to any breed require records that mostly do not exist. Existing data support selected case studies.

operationalization: Across long-cultivated plants, relate genomic and morphological divergence from inferred wild relatives to whether parent stocks were historically recognizable, controlling extinction and sampling. Greater accumulated change associated with failed recognition supports the explanation.
obstacles: Modern genomics can identify parents once unrecognizable morphologically.
Extinction and unsampled wild diversity are rival explanations.
rationale: Crop genomics can now infer many parent stocks and quantify divergence, but cannot cleanly recover nineteenth-century recognizability or exclude lost ancestors. The proposed causal explanation is therefore only partly testable.

operationalization: Measure standardized among-breed variance in external morphology and internal anatomy across domestic species, then compare their effect-size distributions. Consistently larger external divergence supports the claim; similar internal divergence refutes it.
obstacles: External and internal traits have no natural common scale.
Internal anatomy is sampled far less densely.
rationale: The distinction can be quantified and relevant public resources exist, but internal measurements are sparse and trait scaling is consequential. Current data cover a subset of domestic animals.

operationalization: Estimate the probability of observing beneficial variants as a function of census or screened population size while controlling mutation rate and selection protocol. A rising discovery probability and stronger selection response with larger samples supports the claim.
obstacles: Breeding programs differ in effort and genetic diversity.
Useful variants are context dependent.
rationale: The sampling prediction follows directly from rare-variant probability and is testable in many archived breeding and experimental datasets. Full taxonomic scope is unnecessary to discriminate the stated mechanism.

operationalization: Across domestic lineages, partition phenotypic change among selection, drift, environment, use, correlation and crossing using genomic time series and pedigrees. Selection explaining a clearly larger share than each rival supports predominance.
obstacles: Causal components overlap and are not additive.
Representative historical time series are scarce.
rationale: Selection signatures are widespread, but a common causal accounting across all domestic plants and animals is not available. Existing data can evaluate predominance in individual lineages only.

operationalization: Measure heritable within-species differences and test whether selection differentials on them predict allele-frequency or trait shifts across generations. Repeatable directional accumulation supports the mechanism; absence of heritable variation or response refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: public field selection and quantitative-genetic datasets

obstacles: Field selection estimates can be environmentally confounded.
Well-studied taxa are nonrandom.
rationale: Heritable variation and evolutionary response are standard measurable quantities represented in many open datasets. Existing evidence spans enough systems for a strong test of the mechanism, though not every species.

operationalization: Within polymorphic genera, estimate fitness effects and selection gradients for highly variable structures, comparing them with less variable traits. Near-zero effects coupled with persistent variation support the claim; consistent positive or negative selection refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence and taxonomic records for polymorphic genera

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: trait and fitness datasets from individual studies

obstacles: Fitness effects are environment dependent.
Trait-fitness data for the named genera are sparse.
rationale: Neutrality is operationalizable but requires direct fitness data, not merely high variation. Public observations and study datasets permit limited tests, while the general causal attribution remains confounded.

operationalization: Classify taxonomically disputed forms among highly mobile sexual animals and compare their frequency in sympatric versus geographically separated pairs, controlling study effort. A substantially lower within-country frequency supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: geographic occurrence of disputed animal forms

obstacles: Taxonomic disagreement is not encoded uniformly.
Country boundaries are a historical proxy for separation.
rationale: Occurrence and taxonomic resources provide broad coverage, and the spatial comparison is straightforward after defining disputed forms. Curating disagreement is required but feasible within sampled clades.

operationalization: Compile genetic, morphological and reproductive distances from individuals through named varieties, subspecies and species, and test whether any universal discontinuity separates ranks. Continuous overlapping distance distributions support the claim; a robust cross-taxon gap refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: BOLD Systems
candidate_datasets.role: barcode distances linked to taxonomic ranks

obstacles: Taxonomic ranks are partly assigned using the same traits.
Different species concepts imply different boundaries.
rationale: Massive public taxonomic and sequence datasets directly reveal overlap among ranks. Circularity limits some comparisons, but independent reproductive and genomic metrics can provide a decisive test of a universal clear line.

operationalization: Use genomic and phenotypic time series of diverging populations to test whether selection progressively increases stable differentiation and reproductive isolation beyond drift and gene-flow models. Directional accumulation ending in isolation supports the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: population genomic data across divergence continua

obstacles: Most speciation histories lack temporal observations.
Selection and reduced gene flow can be difficult to separate.
rationale: Many divergence continua can be analyzed with public genomic data, but they are snapshots and taxonomically biased. They test pathways in selected systems rather than the general progression asserted.

operationalization: The assertion concerns how taxonomic words are defined and whether ranks possess an 'essential' distinction; observed continuity can motivate it but cannot empirically decide a stipulative classification convention.
obstacles: 'Arbitrary' and 'essentially different' are conceptual terms.
Any observed pattern is compatible with redefining species or variety.
rationale: Datasets can measure discontinuities among organisms but cannot establish that a naming convention is arbitrary in the intended philosophical sense. No empirical outcome uniquely resolves the claim as stated.

operationalization: Model the number or probability of recognized infraspecific varieties as a function of range size, occupancy and abundance across regional floras, controlling sampling and taxonomy. Positive associations for all three dominance measures support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: range, occupancy and occurrence-based abundance proxies

candidate_datasets.name: Plants of the World Online
candidate_datasets.role: accepted plant species and infraspecific taxa

obstacles: Sampling effort inflates both range and recorded varieties.
Abundance is poorly estimated by opportunistic occurrences.
rationale: Global occurrence and plant taxonomic resources directly support a broad modern replication. Bias-aware hierarchical models can discriminate the predicted association, although abundance remains a proxy.

operationalization: Within regions and major clades, regress the proportion of species with accepted varieties and varieties per varying species on genus species richness, controlling sampling effort. A consistent positive relationship supports the claim; zero or negative effects refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: genus sizes and accepted infraspecific taxa

obstacles: Taxonomic effort is greater in species-rich genera.
Variety rank is used unevenly among clades.
rationale: The variables are directly represented in global public taxonomic databases and analysis is simple. Replication across regions and clades can expose taxonomic-practice confounding.

operationalization: Reconstruct genus richness through stratigraphic time from fossil occurrences and estimate transitions from small to large and trajectories after peak richness. Frequent large expansions of initially small genera and peak-to-extinction declines support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences and genus richness through time

obstacles: Preservation and collection effort vary through time.
Genus concepts change taxonomically.
rationale: The Paleobiology Database directly supports genus-level richness trajectories over extensive intervals. Sampling-standardization methods make the qualitative historical propositions testable despite fossil bias.

operationalization: Estimate current incipient-speciation rates from genomic divergence, reproductive isolation and lineage splitting, then test whether they increase with existing genus richness after age and sampling controls. A positive average relationship supports the prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: population genomic evidence of ongoing divergence

obstacles: 'Still forming' is not directly observable.
Genus age and taxonomic practice strongly confound richness.
rationale: Current divergence can proxy species formation in well-sampled clades, but no global dataset consistently identifies incipient species. Available data test restricted groups and depend on contested speciation metrics.

operationalization: Compare standardized pairwise genetic and morphological distances among species in large versus small genera, with phylogenetic age and sampling controls. Smaller within-genus distances in large genera support the claim.
obstacles: Large genera may be younger or taxonomically oversplit.
Morphological coverage is uneven.
rationale: Sequence databases provide millions of comparable species distances and taxonomies provide genus sizes. The predicted contrast can be tested quickly and robustly across clades.

operationalization: Quantify imbalance and multimodality of within-genus phylogenetic or phenotypic distances in large genera against equal-dispersion null models. Recurrent tight subclusters around central or ancestral forms support the claim.
obstacles: A 'central species' needs an explicit definition.
Taxonomic splitting itself creates clusters.
rationale: Public trees and sequences directly encode unequal relatedness among species. Several defensible clustering statistics can test the core assertion broadly, despite ambiguity about satellites.

operationalization: Relate each species' range size to its nearest-neighbor genetic or phylogenetic distance, controlling clade, latitude and observation effort. Smaller ranges among closest relatives support the claim; no or opposite association refutes it.
obstacles: Occurrence-derived ranges are sensitive to sampling.
Recent species may have small ranges for reasons unrelated to variety status.
rationale: Global occurrences and phylogenies make both variables available across many taxa. The association and major confounds can be assessed with standard comparative models.

operationalization: Compare the joint observed patterns of genus size, infraspecific variation, relatedness and range size under explicit branching-descent models versus independent-origin models. Strong likelihood or predictive advantage for descent supports the inference.
obstacles: Independent creation has no agreed probabilistic model.
The listed analogies are not independent of taxonomy.
rationale: The analogies are measurable and descent makes quantitative clustering predictions, but 'utterly inexplicable' is not a well-specified rival. Existing data strongly assess comparative fit without logically excluding every creation model.

operationalization: Using fossil and dated phylogenetic time slices, test whether initially species-rich genera have higher subsequent net diversification and whether widespread abundant lineages leave more dominant descendants. Positive temporal effects support the prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: genus richness trajectories through geological time

obstacles: Survivorship bias can create apparent rich-get-richer patterns.
Dominance has no single cross-taxon measure.
rationale: Genus growth is testable with fossil data, but connecting it causally to present dominance and modified dominant descendants requires proxies. Different components are resolvable to different degrees.

operationalization: Compare potential population growth from fecundity and survival schedules with observed long-run abundance, and quantify density-, enemy- or environment-dependent mortality. Potential production exceeding realized recruitment with limiting mortality supports the mechanism.
obstacles: Microbes and many invertebrates are underrepresented.
'Struggle' requires mapping to measurable density dependence or mortality.
rationale: Demographic matrices directly estimate growth potential and realized limitation across many plants and animals. The universal wording exceeds coverage, but the central mechanism has clear and broadly testable consequences.

operationalization: For dated introductions, fit spread and abundance trajectories using intrinsic growth, fertility in native versus introduced ranges, and stage-specific mortality. Rapid spread explained by reduced mortality without increased fertility supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species

obstacles: A specific dataset URL may not encode abundance or demography.
Introduction dates and early absences are uncertain.
Enemy release, adaptation and propagule pressure are confounded.
rationale: Spread data are extensive, but paired fertility and mortality data are available only for selected invasions. Thus exponential spread is testable broadly while the asserted exclusive demographic explanation is only partially resolvable.

operationalization: Across species, model equilibrium abundance from fecundity and stage-specific mortality, testing whether fecundity effects vanish after early mortality and other vital rates are included. Weak direct effects and compensation by destruction support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: COMPADRE Plant Matrix Database
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity and stage-specific plant vital rates

obstacles: Matrix databases rarely measure absolute field abundance.
Vital-rate estimates are taxonomically biased.
rationale: Public demographic matrices contain the needed life-history variables for many species, but often not abundance measured on matching populations. Restricted comparative tests are feasible.

operationalization: Across animal population time series, compare variance and density dependence attributable to prey resources versus predator abundance using lagged causal models or removals. More populations primarily limited by predation would support 'very frequently.'
obstacles: Food and predator time series rarely accompany focal abundance.
Top-down and bottom-up effects interact and share climate drivers.
rationale: Population and interaction databases identify candidate systems, but the causal covariates needed to distinguish predation from food limitation are sparse. Existing data can resolve selected long-term studies only.

operationalization: Link population growth and crash events to standardized cold and drought extremes, then compare their effect sizes with predation, disease, competition and ordinary resource limitation. Extremes having the largest recurrent effects supports the superlative claim.
obstacles: Biotic checks are measured less consistently than weather.
Extreme events and biological responses are spatially mismatched.
rationale: Abundance and climate archives enable broad event studies, but ranking climate as the most effective of all checks requires consistently measured rivals that are usually absent. The climate effect is more resolvable than the superlative.

operationalization: Along replicated latitude and elevation gradients, test whether species richness declines and whether organism size or performance is more directly predicted by climate where competitor richness is low. The full linked pattern supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: species richness and organism occurrences along gradients

obstacles: Trait data access and coverage are uneven.
Latitude, elevation and climate covary with productivity and history.
rationale: Richness and climate gradients are exceptionally well covered, but attributing stunting directly to climate rather than competition requires trait and experimental evidence. Components can be tested broadly, the causal chain only partially.

operationalization: For introduced garden plants that survive cultivation, model naturalization success from abiotic climatic suitability and measured competition or herbivory. Strong biotic effects after high abiotic suitability supports mainly indirect limitation.
obstacles: Non-naturalization may reflect propagule pressure.
Competition and herbivory are not globally measured.
rationale: Naturalization and climate data permit the abiotic component to be modeled globally, but direct biotic covariates are limited to experiments and local studies. The 'mainly' causal comparison is therefore restricted.

operationalization: Estimate persistence probability against conspecific density and enemy density across populations, looking for a positive threshold or Allee effect; then test whether range-restricted plants have high abundance within occupied sites. A widespread enemy-relative threshold supports the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: range restriction and local occurrence density proxies

obstacles: Enemy and absolute density time series are rarely paired.
Opportunistic occurrences cannot identify persistence thresholds.
rationale: The mechanism has a clear density-dependent test, but current global datasets provide only coarse proxies. Adequate replicated population-enemy time series would need to be collected or compiled from new observations.

operationalization: Quantify long-term turnover and compositional stability in communities while measuring interaction-strength fluctuations, and test whether small perturbations predict persistent state shifts. Low net turnover despite fluctuating interactions plus high sensitivity would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Long Term Ecological Research Network Data Portal

obstacles: Most records are decades, not evolutionary long periods.
Fine balance of opposing forces is not directly observed.
rationale: Community stability is well represented in public time series, but the inferred mechanism and sensitivity to trifling changes are hard to distinguish from environmental stationarity. Present data resolve modern restricted versions.

operationalization: Fit a mediated causal model in systems with predator, intermediate consumer, pollinator and plant abundance time series, testing whether predator changes propagate through the specified links to plant frequency. A significant signed indirect effect supports the chain.
obstacles: Interaction records rarely align with abundance through time.
Shared environmental drivers can mimic cascades.
rationale: Interaction networks and community time series identify candidate chains, and some trophic cascades have open experimental data. The specific complete causal sequence is rarely observed at suitable resolution.

operationalization: Compare per-capita fitness effects of increasing conspecific, same-species-variety and heterospecific density across replicated field or experimental communities. Consistently largest negative effects from conspecific density support the claim.
obstacles: Comparable intra- and interspecific manipulations are sparse.
Natural enemies can generate apparent conspecific density dependence.
rationale: Competition coefficients are directly estimable, but no broad integrated public dataset compares all competitor classes across organisms. Meta-analysis of archived studies can test subsets with substantial harmonization.

operationalization: Across competition experiments, compare interaction coefficients for congeneric species pairs with matched noncongeneric pairs, controlling functional similarity, environment and phylogenetic distance. Stronger average congeneric suppression supports the claim.
obstacles: Published interaction datasets are biased toward strong effects.
Congeneric status conflates relatedness with niche similarity.
rationale: The comparison is clear and many individual datasets exist, but effect estimates require substantial compilation and cover limited taxa. Existing evidence can test a restricted meta-analytic version.

operationalization: Across documented interactions, test whether organismal structures covary with corresponding competitor, predator, prey or escape-related structures after phylogenetic and environmental controls. Reciprocal functional matching supports the relational claim.
obstacles: 'Every organism' and 'most essential' are not exhaustively testable.
Trait matching does not by itself establish causal shaping.
rationale: Trait matching can be tested for many interaction classes, but joining morphology to interaction records is incomplete and causal coevolution is confounded by shared environments. The universal formulation is beyond current coverage.
